verses.text: A psalm for reflection by Asaph. Listen to what I’m teaching you, my people. Lean in and hear what I’m saying.
I’ll tell you a parable and speak the hard-to-understand sayings from long ago,
things we’ve heard and known because our ancestors told us.
We won’t keep them from their children. We’ll tell the next generation what makes the LORD worthy of praise, how strong he is, and what wonders he’s done.
He established a covenant in Jacob and gave Israel his teaching. He told our ancestors to pass it on to their children,
so the next generation would know it, even the children who weren’t born yet. Then they’d grow up and tell their own children.
That way they’d put their hope in God, remember what he’s done, and keep his commands.
They wouldn’t turn out like their ancestors, stubborn and rebellious, with hearts that wouldn’t stay loyal and spirits that wouldn’t stick with God.
Ephraim’s people had their bows ready, but when battle came, they turned back.
They broke God’s covenant and refused to live by his instruction.
They forgot what he’d done and all the wonders he’d shown them.
He did amazing things right in front of their ancestors in Egypt, in the fields of Zoan.
He split the sea and led them through it. He piled up the water so it stood in place.
By day he led them with a cloud. All night he led them with the light of fire.
He split rocks in the wilderness and gave them water like it was pouring from the depths.
He made streams gush out of the rock, and water ran down like rivers.
Still they kept sinning against him and rebelling against the Most High in the desert.
In their hearts they put God to the test by demanding the food they craved.
They talked against God and said, “Can God spread a table out here in the wilderness?
Sure, he struck the rock and water gushed out until streams overflowed. But can he give us bread too? Can he give his people meat?”
The LORD heard them and was furious. A fire flared up against Jacob, and anger rose against Israel,
because they didn’t believe God or trust him to save them.
Even so, he gave orders to the skies above and opened heaven’s doors.
He rained down manna for them to eat. He gave them food from the sky.
People ate the bread of angels. He sent them all the food they could eat.
He made the east wind blow across the sky and steered the south wind by his power.
He rained meat down like dust, birds as countless as sand by the sea.
He dropped them right in the middle of the camp, all around their homes.
The people ate until they were full. He gave them what they craved.
They still hadn’t let go of their cravings. The food was still in their mouths
when God’s anger rose against them. He killed some of their strongest and struck down Israel’s young men.
After all that, they still sinned and refused to believe in his wonders.
So he let their days come to nothing and their years pass in terror.
When he struck them down, they started looking for him. They turned back and sought God in earnest.
They remembered that God was their rock, that God Most High was the one who redeemed them.
But they just tried to flatter him. The words on their tongues were lies.
Their hearts weren’t right with him, and they didn’t stay faithful to his covenant.
But he had mercy. He forgave their wrongdoing and spared them. Again and again he turned his anger away and held back the full force of his wrath.
He remembered they were only flesh, like a gust of wind that passes and never comes back.
How often they rebelled against him in the wilderness and caused him grief in the desert!
Again they put God to the test and provoked the Holy One of Israel.
They forgot the power of his hand and the day he rescued them from their enemy.
They forgot the signs he performed in Egypt and the wonders he showed in the fields of Zoan.
He turned their rivers and streams into blood, so they couldn’t drink from them.
He sent swarms of flies that devoured them and frogs that brought ruin.
He gave their crops to caterpillars and everything they’d worked for to locusts.
He wrecked their vines with hail and their sycamore fig trees with frost.
He handed their livestock over to the hail and their flocks to blazing thunderbolts.
He unleashed the full heat of his anger on them, wrath, indignation, and trouble, with a band of angels bringing disaster.
He cleared a path for his anger. He didn’t spare their lives from death. He handed them over to plague.
He struck down every firstborn in Egypt, the first of their strength in the tents of Ham.
But he led his own people out like sheep and guided them through the wilderness like a flock.
He led them safely, so they had no reason to fear. The sea swept over their enemies.
He brought them to the edge of his holy land, to this mountain his right hand had won.
He drove out the nations ahead of them, measured out their inheritance, and settled the tribes of Israel in their tents.
Still they tested and rebelled against God Most High. They refused to keep his commands.
They turned back and betrayed him like their ancestors. They were as unreliable as a warped bow.
They angered him with their high places and stirred up his jealousy with their carved idols.
God heard and was furious. He rejected Israel outright.
He left the tent at Shiloh, the tent he’d set up among people.
He let his strength be taken captive and handed his glory over to the enemy.
He handed his people over to the sword. He was angry with his own inheritance.
Fire devoured their young men, and their young women had no wedding songs.
Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows couldn’t even weep.
Then the Lord rose like someone waking from sleep, like a warrior shouting after drinking wine.
He struck his enemies and drove them back, putting them to shame forever.
He rejected Joseph’s tent and passed over the tribe of Ephraim.
He chose the tribe of Judah and Mount Zion, which he loved.
He built his sanctuary high like the heavens, firm like the earth he’s established forever.
He chose David as his servant and took him from the sheep pens.
He called him away from tending sheep with their lambs to shepherd Jacob, his people, and Israel, his inheritance.
David shepherded them with an honest heart and guided them with skillful hands.
